notes: Seed edition composed by Claude from the 448 collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each reading commits to a claim. The last rung of every reading argues against it. Read both.
Connections are the oracle's, not the publishers'. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.

Each reading ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, the past decade, the past fifty years, since September 2001 and since 1945, that place the day's pattern on longer trajectories. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads. Every link has been checked.

readings.line: A ballot cast in Brazil is being counted in Buenos Aires, Madrid and Nairobi.
readings.claim: Lula's re-election is the most reported event in this collection, and almost none of the reporting is about Brazil. Within a day the result has been made into an argument in Argentina, a warning in Chile, a model in Spain, a hope in Kenya and a fraud in Washington. An election no longer ends at a border. It is a script that other countries pick up and perform.

rungs.label: The result leaves Brazil within hours

fragments.label: The neighbours read it as their own future
fragments.text: A Chilean editorial says Brazil has forced Chile and the United States to look at the region anew, and Chile's president congratulates Lula on their shared future. In Argentina, Axel Kicillof says the defeat of Bolsonaro is a rejection of Milei's chainsaw. Nobody is describing Brazil. Everybody is describing themselves.

fragments.label: Europe and Spain draft a partnership
fragments.text: German reporting has European parliamentarians already envisaging a partnership with Lula's Brazil. An Asturian columnist writes that Sánchez follows in Lula's footsteps. The result is a day old and it is already a foreign policy and a domestic parable.

rungs.label: Denial has a passport now

fragments.label: 'Rigged' is said in Washington, printed in Athens
fragments.text: Two Greek outlets lead with Trump calling Brazil's election rigged. Flávio Bolsonaro says he will seek the disqualification of Lula's ticket, then that the police took his passport, then that he will drop the annulment and pursue an abuse-of-power case instead. The sequence is familiar because it has been performed before, in Washington in 2021 and in Brasília in 2023.

fragments.label: Jerusalem rehearses for a genre
fragments.text: Israel's police are bracing for a 'January 6 scenario' at the Knesset after their own election. The date has become a noun. A country that has not yet voted is preparing for the thing that happens after a vote is refused.

rungs.label: The market casts the second vote

fragments.label: The real falls on the news that the people chose
fragments.text: Al Jazeera and Finland's Yle both lead with the currency: Brazil's real sinks and its shares plunge after the result. This is the double movement Polanyi described. Society votes one way and capital votes the other, within the same twenty-four hours, and both results are real.

fragments.label: Only one outlet is still counting
fragments.text: Of all the headlines about this election, the only one that is about the votes themselves is Brazilian: R7's live count. Everyone else moved on to what it means before the counting finished. The event is the smallest part of the story.

rungs.label: Elections are now a catalogue of models

fragments.label: Kenya shops for a miracle
fragments.text: In Nairobi, Edwin Sifuna banks on 'electoral miracles' in 2027 and cites Serbia and Brazil in one sentence. Serbia's students have just defeated Vučić after fourteen years; Italy and Spain are both asking who they are. The world has a shelf of recent results, and politicians in countries that have not voted yet are choosing one to imitate.

fragments.label: The same week, everyone is voting
fragments.text: Bulgaria's president finishes first in a first round. Al Jazeera explains the US midterms. Ontario's premier says he can't wait for them. An election in one country is now a season in all of them, and the same vocabulary is used for each.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: Elections have always been read abroad
fragments.text: Foreign newspapers wrote about Allende, Mitterrand and Mandela within a day. What looks like contagion may just be the ordinary interest of neighbours, made visible because this collection sorts headlines by country. The claim that something has changed needs a comparison this snapshot cannot supply.

fragments.label: Lula says the opposite
fragments.text: The one Lula quote in the collection is 'Brazil is nobody's backyard'. The reading says the election belongs to everyone. The man who won it says it belongs to Brazil. If he is right, the foreign framing is noise, and the oracle has mistaken the echo for the event.

horizons.text: The decade began with two results that were read everywhere at once, Brexit in June 2016 and Trump in November, and it taught politicians that a foreign election is a free rehearsal. Brazil then ran the whole script in miniature: Lula jailed in 2018 under a conviction later annulled, Bolsonaro elected that October, Lula back by fewer than two points in 2022, the storming of the three powers on 8 January 2023, Bolsonaro barred from office and then convicted in 2025 of plotting a coup. Each step was watched from Buenos Aires and Washington as a preview. Milei's win in 2023 was read as Brazil's warning, and Lula's win this week is being read as Milei's. Serbia's students started with a collapsed station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024 and ended, by these headlines, with a government. The decade's lesson is that results are portable, and so is the refusal of results.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: Fifty years ago most of the countries in this constellation did not hold real elections. Portugal's revolution of 1974 opened what Huntington later called the third wave: Spain in 1977, Argentina in 1983, Chile's plebiscite in 1988, Brazil's first direct presidential vote in 1989 and the fall of the Eastern bloc the same year. The wave created an industry of observers, exit polls and foreign commentary, and it coincided with the freeing of capital. When Lula first looked likely to win, in 2002, the real lost a third of its value before a vote was cast and he had to publish a letter promising to honour Brazil's debts. The market's second vote, which Al Jazeera and Yle report falling on Monday morning, has been cast in every Brazilian election since. Kenya's multi-party politics date from 1991 and Serbia's from 1990. The countries now reading each other's results are mostly countries that learned to vote in the same thirty years, with the same consultants, under the same markets.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: After 2001 the export of elections became a security policy, and its failure in Iraq discredited the exporters without ending the traffic. The colour revolutions of 2003 to 2005 in Georgia, Ukraine and Kyrgyzstan borrowed Otpor's Belgrade manual directly; Russia answered with a foreign-agents law in 2012 and a theory that every crowd abroad is somebody's project. Social media then made the reading instantaneous. The 2016 American election was contested as a foreign operation, and 'rigged', shouted in Washington in 2020, was repeated in Brasília in 2022 and 2023 and is being printed in Athens this week about Brazil. Sifuna's 'electoral miracles' in Nairobi and Israel's police drill for a 'January 6 scenario' are the same phenomenon seen from two sides: an outcome and its refusal have both become templates. Krastev and Holmes called the thirty years after 1989 the age of imitation. The imitation now runs in every direction, and it includes the losing.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: The idea that an election anywhere is everybody's business is a postwar invention with two authors. One is Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of 1948, which made periodic and genuine elections a human right. The other is the Cold War, which made them a battlefield. Washington funded the Italian centre in 1948, helped remove elected governments in Iran in 1953 and Guatemala in 1954, backed Brazil's generals in 1964 and set out to make Chile's economy scream after Allende won in 1970. Moscow ran its own version on its own side. For forty years an election abroad was read seriously in two capitals. What this collection shows is the same habit democratised: Nairobi, Athens, Oviedo and Amman all read Brazil's result as news about themselves, without any of them being able to do much about it. Anderson wrote that nations imagined themselves by reading the same newspaper on the same morning. On this morning the paper is the same in forty countries, and the nation it imagines does not have a name yet.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: A company has written down the end of the world as a risk factor, and the market has bought it.
readings.claim: An AI company's listing documents devote a hundred pages to risk, including human extinction, and semiconductor stocks rise on the news. Three continents report it the same day. This is the strangest fact in the collection: total disclosure of the worst case has become a form of confidence. The future arrives as somebody else's maintenance, and the market pays for the arrival, not the maintenance.

rungs.label: The confession is the prospectus

fragments.label: A hundred pages of what could go wrong
fragments.text: Fortune reads Anthropic's S-1 and finds human extinction, the Pentagon and the founder's reputation listed as risks. Taiwan's United Daily News counts nearly a hundred pages of them, from TSMC supply to AI threatening survival. The document that is supposed to sell the company spends most of its length describing how it could end everything.

fragments.label: The index jumps on the warning
fragments.text: The same Taiwanese outlet reports the US close: listing plans ignite AI buying, the semiconductor index jumps 2.8 percent, doubts remain. In Shanghai, Sina quotes Citadel saying the AI trade has reached a staggering scale with no room for error. The worst case was priced in and the price went up.

rungs.label: The opposite of Theranos is not honesty

fragments.label: A deception expert and one word
fragments.text: On the same day, Fortune reports Elizabeth Holmes insisting she never lied, and a deception expert says the whole case hinges on one tiny word. Theranos sold a future with no disclosure. The new prospectus sells a future with total disclosure. Both ask money to believe in something that has not happened yet. The amount of confession is not the same as the amount of truth.

rungs.label: The future arrives as somebody else's maintenance

fragments.label: A composer is asked to fix the machine's music
fragments.text: An Australian headline: the Artful Dodger soundtrack composer is asked to fix AI music. A Korean one: semiconductor exports drive a full point of GDP growth. An American one asks why data centres use so much water. The generated thing is cheap. The repairing, the fabricating and the cooling are done by people and rivers who did not file an S-1.

fragments.label: Sixty thousand people are offered the door
fragments.text: Microsoft offers voluntary departures to about sixty thousand employees, a quarter of its workforce, in Taiwanese reporting. SolarEdge lays off another nine hundred. The boom's labour market is exits, not hires. Hirschman's choice is being made at scale: leave quietly, because voice has nowhere to go.

rungs.label: The public was not asked, and says so

fragments.label: Six in ten say too fast
fragments.text: Six in ten Dutch people believe AI is becoming part of society too quickly. An Australian columnist says big tech is destroying democracy and political cowards are letting it. A Portuguese outlet reports US midterm candidates trying to manipulate chatbots into recommending them. The machine is being voted on, by people who were not given a ballot.

fragments.label: Twelve machines are asked about us
fragments.text: A Ukrainian outlet reports that twelve AI models were asked a question about humans and almost all agreed on one uncomfortable truth. The headline does not say what it was. That is the most honest headline in the collection: the oracle is being consulted, and the answer is withheld for clicks.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: This is how every technology arrives
fragments.text: Railways needed navvies, electricity needed linesmen, the car needed roads paid for by everyone. 'Somebody else's maintenance' describes all infrastructure, not AI in particular. To make the claim stick you would have to show that the gap between who profits and who repairs is wider now than it was for the telegraph. Nothing here measures that.

fragments.label: The hundred pages are a legal form, not a confession
fragments.text: Every US listing lists catastrophic risks because lawyers require it. Reading a boilerplate section as a philosophical statement is the oracle hearing meaning in a compliance document. The market rose because of expected revenue, and the extinction clause is a footnote the reporters chose for its headline value.

horizons.text: In March 2016 a machine beat Lee Sedol at Go, and the decade's story started as a demonstration. It became a market in November 2022, when ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months and Nvidia, until then a graphics company, passed a trillion dollars in value six months later. The warning travelled with the product. In 2019 OpenAI withheld a model as too dangerous to release, which doubled as the best advertisement it ever ran; in May 2023 the heads of the main laboratories signed a one-sentence statement that extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. This week's prospectus is that sentence moved from an open letter into a legal filing, which is the decade's whole arc: alarm as part of the pitch. Underneath it the physical bill arrived. Data centres competing with towns for water and power, a chip supply resting on one island, and a labour market in which the boom's largest employer offers exits rather than hires.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: Every technology of the last fifty years has reached the public through a prospectus, and the prospectus has grown longer each time. Apple listed in 1980 and Microsoft in 1986 with risk sections of a few pages. Netscape's listing in 1995 priced the internet before the company had a profit and opened five years in which disclosure was no obstacle to belief; the crash of 2000 erased trillions and produced the Sarbanes-Oxley rules of 2002 that make today's hundred pages mandatory. Google in 2004 added a founders' letter promising not to be evil, the first prospectus to sell a conscience. Theranos, which never listed, showed what happens with no disclosure at all. The labour side has a parallel history. The voluntary departure, the buyout and the restructuring entered the vocabulary in the 1980s, when General Electric shed a quarter of its workforce and was praised for it. Microsoft's offer to sixty thousand people is that playbook at the scale of a boom rather than a slump. Hirschman's exit has become a product the employer sells back to the employee.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: Zuboff's argument is that the business model behind this boom was born in the weeks after September 2001, when a government that had wanted to regulate what Google knew decided instead that it wanted to know it too. Data collection became a civic duty, the Patriot Act gave it cover, and advertising paid for it. The smartphone in 2007 and the cloud after 2008 turned that collection into infrastructure. Snowden in 2013 and Cambridge Analytica in 2018 were the public's two chances to object; Europe answered with the GDPR, America with hearings. The chips tell the other half. The crisis of 2008 pushed manufacturing to the cheapest fab, which became Taiwan's TSMC, and the export controls and CHIPS Act of 2022 turned a supply chain into a front line, which is why a Taiwanese paper reads an American prospectus for its mention of TSMC first. Rosa's point about acceleration fits here: each cycle has been shorter than the last, and six in ten Dutch respondents now report feeling the speed before anyone can name the harm.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: The first technology tested with an explicit estimate that it might end the world went off in the New Mexico desert on 16 July 1945, after a physicist had checked the arithmetic on whether it would ignite the atmosphere and found that it would not. That was a state project, paid for by taxes and kept secret. Computing grew in its shadow: ENIAC the same year, Turing's question in 1950, the Dartmouth workshop that named artificial intelligence in 1956, ARPA founded after Sputnik in 1958. For forty years the technologies that could change everything were built by governments and argued about in parliaments. The shift since is not that the risks are larger but that the builder is a company and the public forum is a securities filing. Beck wrote in 1986, the year of Chernobyl, that modern societies had begun producing risks they could not insure and then arguing about who should bear them. A prospectus that lists extinction and asks for money is that argument in its purest form: the risk is socialised, the upside is listed, and the reader is invited to buy.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: The Gulf is running two clocks: one for the talks, one for the strike.
readings.claim: In the same collection, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to keep talking, Iran says it is ready to join the Mecca Pact, and an Iraqi paper reports that Washington has completed preparations for a large-scale strike on Iran. Both are true at once. The region is negotiating with itself in one room while the room next door is being armed, and the headlines from Cairo, Jakarta, Beijing, Tokyo and Doha each hear only one of the clocks.

rungs.label: The first clock: a pact being written

fragments.label: Four countries in one room
fragments.text: Egypt's Masrawy, Shanghai's Yicai and Japan's 47NEWS all report the same meeting: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to discuss regional peace and security. Iran's president says he is ready to deepen cooperation and resolve differences. Republika in Jakarta runs it as breaking news: Iran ready to join the Mecca Pact. The religiously and politically opposed powers of the region are drafting something together.

fragments.label: Doha hears both clocks in one sentence
fragments.text: Al Jazeera Arabic is the only outlet that puts the two clocks in one headline: the Mecca Pact countries and Tehran agree to continue talks as Trump weighs his options. The phrase 'weighs his options' is the second clock, ticking inside the first.

rungs.label: The second clock: a strike being prepared

fragments.label: Baghdad reports the preparations are complete
fragments.text: Iraq's Al-Mada reports that Washington has completed preparations for a large-scale military strike on Iran. A Chinese financial outlet runs a breaking bundle: a multinational coalition launches air strikes, major news from the Strait of Hormuz, the US military ready for another round. Arab News carries Israel's defence minister denying a rift with his army chief over Iran. Three countries that are not Iran are reporting the countdown.

fragments.label: The war has already reached the departure board
fragments.text: Al-Mada: 86 percent of flights cancelled as Houthis disrupt Riyadh airport. South Africa's Business Day explains how Houthi attacks have grounded flights across Saudi Arabia. Xinhua reports the Saudi-led coalition intercepting drones and a ballistic missile. Whatever the strike clock says, the airport clock has already stopped.

rungs.label: A church is the thing that makes a state move

fragments.label: Jordan bombs Syria for a church
fragments.text: Four outlets on three continents, Xinhua, Deutsche Welle, a Greek daily and Arab News, report Jordan's air strikes in southern Syria after a deadly attack on a church. Only the Greek paper names it as a Greek Orthodox church. The BBC reports sixty Orthodox Christians killed in Ethiopia the same day. In a region of pacts and strikes, the trigger that actually fired was an attack on worshippers.

fragments.label: Amman explains itself to itself
fragments.text: Jordan's own press is doing something different from the foreign press. Ammon News asks why the security agencies avoided announcing the extent of the terrorists' links, and reports speakers in Aqaba calling Jordan a homeland of love that will withstand terrorism. The strike is the foreign headline. The domestic headline is reassurance.

rungs.label: While the clocks run, the map is being redrawn

fragments.label: Algeria sends soldiers abroad for the first time in half a century
fragments.text: Franceinfo calls it a first in more than fifty years: Algeria authorises sending troops abroad. Deutsche Welle reports the debate; Masrawy reports the destination, Niger. Qatar's emir flies to Moscow to meet Putin. Pakistan and the United States agree on energy. The Gulf's two clocks are the loudest, but the quiet redrawings happen in the Sahara and the Kremlin.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: One of the clocks might be a prop
fragments.text: The 'preparations complete' headline comes from a single Iraqi paper, and the coalition-strikes bundle is a Chinese financial feed summarising unnamed reports. Talks are reported by five outlets, the strike by three second-hand ones. A reading that gives both clocks equal weight has made a sourcing decision disguised as a philosophical one.

fragments.label: Diplomacy under threat is the normal condition
fragments.text: Every serious negotiation happens with force in the next room. That is what makes it serious. Calling it 'two clocks' makes a standard feature of statecraft sound like a paradox. The interesting question is not that both exist, but which one the parties in Tehran believe, and no headline here can tell you.

horizons.text: Both clocks have been running for ten years. The Iran agreement of July 2015 was the pact; the American withdrawal in May 2018 restarted the strike clock, and since then the region has alternated between the two at increasing speed: Houthi drones on the Abqaiq oil plant in September 2019, Soleimani killed in January 2020, the Abraham Accords that September, Saudi Arabia and Iran restoring relations under Chinese sponsorship in March 2023, then 7 October and the Gaza war, Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping, Iran's first direct strikes on Israel in April 2024, the fall of Assad in December 2024, and a twelve-day Israel-Iran war in June 2025 that ended with American bombers over Fordow. Syria is now governed by a man who was on Washington's terrorist list a year before he took power, and Jordan is bombing in southern Syria again, this time for a church. The headlines that read as a contradiction, talks in one room and preparations in the next, describe the only rhythm the region has known since 2015.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: The alliances meeting this week were drawn in 1979. In February the Shah fell; in November armed millenarians seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca and the Saudi state answered with thirty years of religious strictness; in December the Soviet army entered Afghanistan, and in January 1980 Washington declared that it would use force to keep the Gulf's oil flowing. Everything since has been a rearrangement of that year: the Iran-Iraq war, the Gulf Cooperation Council formed in 1981 out of fear of Tehran, Pakistan's bomb and the Saudi money behind it, Turkey's return to a region it had left in 1918. The Saudi-Pakistani defence agreement signed in 2025 formalised a relationship that began with Riyadh paying for Islamabad's arsenal. Algeria, whose army last fought abroad on the Egyptian front in 1973, changed its constitution in 2020 to permit deployments and is now sending troops to Niger, where French and American forces left and Russian ones arrived. Yergin called oil the prize. Fifty years on the prize is still on the table, and the people around it have changed seats.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: The invasion of Iraq in 2003 removed Iran's main enemy and handed Tehran a corridor to the Mediterranean; King Abdullah of Jordan named it the Shia crescent in 2004, and Jordan has lived on that fault line since. The wars that followed, Lebanon in 2006, Syria from 2011, Yemen from 2015, turned the region's Christians from a presence into a casualty list: the Baghdad cathedral massacre of 2010, the Coptic church bombings of 2016 and 2017, a Damascus church in June 2025, and now a church in southern Syria and sixty Orthodox dead in Ethiopia on the same day. The airport is the other post-2001 target. Security theatre was invented for passengers; the Houthis inverted it, striking Abha in 2019 and Abu Dhabi in 2022, and this week grounding most of Riyadh's flights. A departure board is a more honest instrument than a communiqué. Kaldor's new wars were supposed to be fought by militias inside failed states. This one is fought by a militia against a rich state's airports, with a great power weighing its options overhead.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: On 14 February 1945, on his way home from Yalta, Roosevelt met Ibn Saud on a cruiser in the Great Bitter Lake and traded American protection for Saudi oil. That bargain, never written down, is the oldest clock in the room. The second oldest is a pact. In 1955 Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and Britain signed the Baghdad Pact, an anti-Soviet alliance of almost exactly the capitals now reported meeting about regional peace and security; it died when Iraq's monarchy was overthrown in 1958. Suez in 1956 ended Britain's role and began America's. Israel's founding in 1948, Mossadegh's removal in 1953 and the embargo of 1973 fixed the pattern in which every regional settlement was underwritten by an outside power and every outside power eventually tired of it. The novelty in this week's headlines is not the two clocks. It is that the four countries talking in Mecca are talking without a sponsor, while the sponsor's bombers are being counted by a paper in Baghdad. The pact of 1955 was written for Washington. Whatever is being written in 2026 is not.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: One machine is cutting the power, guarding the lake, carrying the wounded, and selling itself.
readings.claim: No single word appears in more headlines across more countries in this collection than 'drone'. It hits five power stations in Sudan, is intercepted over Saudi Arabia, watches the Great Lakes from the American side, rescues a Ukrainian soldier who waited two days, is promised by Hezbollah within three months, and is sold by Israeli and Turkish firms to buyers who are not named. It is not a weapon. It is the sentence structure of the decade.

rungs.label: Four verbs, one object

fragments.label: It cuts the power in Khartoum
fragments.text: The Hindu reports mass outages in Sudan after RSF drones hit five power stations. Al Jazeera reports the UN calling Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid a war crime. Kharkiv's missile strike and Kyiv's metro station are in the same collection. The target of choice is no longer the army. It is the switch that keeps the hospital lit.

fragments.label: It watches a lake between friends
fragments.text: CBC: the United States has put surveillance drones in the Great Lakes, and a border-town mayor isn't happy. Mexico's Vanguardia reports air and ground surveillance reinforced on tracks and roads in Coahuila. The same object that cuts the power in a war also hovers over the calmest border on earth, and the mayor's objection is the only sign anyone finds that strange.

fragments.label: It carries a wounded man out
fragments.text: A Virginia station reports a wounded Ukrainian soldier who waited two days to be rescued, then a drone flew him to safety. The machine that cannot be hit back has become, in the same war, the machine that comes when no one else can. Chamayou's question stands: what happens to courage when the thing that saves you is also the thing that cannot be brave.

fragments.label: It sells itself at a trade fair
fragments.text: Elbit wins a $200 million Asia-Pacific intelligence-gathering deal. ASELSAN's wing-assisted guidance kit completes its first firing test and the Turkish defence industry goes on show at AFRIDEX. Al-Mada reports Hezbollah preparing to produce drones within three months with Iranian funding. Everyone is building, buying or showing. No headline reports anyone declining.

rungs.label: It is grammar, not a weapon

fragments.label: The same object swaps verbs without changing shape
fragments.text: A rifle only shoots. A drone cuts, watches, carries and sells, and it does all four in this one day's headlines without anyone remarking on the range. That is what it means for a technology to have become grammar: it no longer appears as a subject, only as the way other things are done. The last object to do this was the truck.

fragments.label: The old machines are still being launched
fragments.text: Russia launches the missile ship Grozny after five years of building. Australia reveals its first AUKUS nuclear submarine. Ukraine asks for ten percent of the West's air-defence missiles. The ship, the submarine and the missile are the nineteenth and twentieth centuries continuing, at enormous cost, alongside a machine that costs almost nothing. The two arms races do not know about each other yet.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: 'Drone' is a word doing the work of six things
fragments.text: An RSF attack drone, a Great Lakes surveillance aircraft, a Ukrainian evacuation quadcopter and an Elbit intelligence contract share a headline word and almost nothing else. The reading's elegance comes from English using one noun. In the original languages some of these are different words. The oracle may be reading the translation, not the world.

fragments.label: Every tool becomes grammar
fragments.text: Fire cooks, warms, signals and destroys. The claim that the drone is special because it has many verbs would apply to the horse. What would make the drone different is cost and distance: anyone can send one and nobody has to be there. That is Chamayou's point, and it is a different and sharper claim than the one the oracle made.

horizons.text: In 2020 Azerbaijan won a war in forty-four days with Turkish and Israeli drones against Armenian armour, and every defence ministry rewrote its shopping list. Ukraine then turned the drone from a weapon into an industry: first-person-view quadcopters built in workshops by the million, a strike in June 2025 launched from lorries parked inside Russia, and, as this week's Virginia station reports, a machine sent to carry a wounded man out. Russia answered with Iranian Shaheds against the grid, which the UN now calls a war crime. Sudan's war, begun in April 2023, is the first in which a militia without an air force has taken a capital's power stations out from the air. The cost curve runs the wrong way for the defender: an interceptor costs a hundred times the thing it destroys. That arithmetic is why Hezbollah plans a factory, why Elbit and ASELSAN are selling, and why the only person objecting in the whole collection is a mayor on the Great Lakes who did not expect the machine to turn up at home.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: The drone's fifty years are an Israeli, American and then Turkish story. Israel flew camera drones after 1973 and, in the Bekaa Valley in June 1982, used them to find and blind Syria's air defences in an afternoon, the first battle the object won. An Israeli-born engineer in California built the Predator's ancestor in a garage in the 1980s; it flew over Bosnia in 1995. The civilian branch waited for the sky to open: in May 2000 the United States switched off the deliberate error in GPS, and within a decade a Shenzhen firm had put a camera on a quadcopter anybody could buy. Turkey, refused American drones in the 2000s, built its own and now shows them at a fair in Africa. The export market in the headlines, Elbit's $200 million deal, Hezbollah's factory, is the fifty-year arc compressed: a thing three countries could make is now a thing any country with an electronics bazaar can field. The old machines in the same collection, a frigate five years in the building and a nuclear submarine, belong to the century in which only states could afford to fight.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: The first armed Predator strike, in Afghanistan in October 2001, created a new kind of act: killing with no possibility of being killed. Over the next fifteen years the United States ran several hundred strikes in Pakistan, Yemen and Somalia, killed one of its own citizens by drone in 2011, invented the 'signature strike' against people whose names it did not know, and in 2013 delivered a presidential speech explaining the rules. Chamayou's book is a reply to that speech. Then the monopoly ended. Islamic State dropped grenades from hobby quadcopters over Mosul in 2016; by 2022 both sides in Ukraine were flying them in thousands. The law moved more slowly than the machine. Protocol I of 1977 already forbids attacking the things a civilian population needs to survive, and the UN's finding that strikes on Ukraine's grid are war crimes applies a 1977 rule to a 2026 weapon. The same decades put drones on the American border: Predators over Mexico from 2005, over the Canadian line from 2009. The Great Lakes mayor is objecting to something that has been overhead for seventeen years.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: The postwar laws of war were written by people who had just watched what aircraft do to cities. Dresden, Tokyo and Hiroshima were the context for the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and the protocols of 1977 tried to put the civilian and the power station outside the target list. The drone's first ancestor flew before any of that: the V-1 of 1944, a pilotless bomb aimed at London by a state that could not spare pilots. The Cold War then made distance the norm. A missile crew in Nebraska and a bomber over the Arctic were already killing without presence, in theory, for forty years. What Nuremberg added in 1945 was the principle that the person who pulls the lever answers for it, and that principle now reaches the pilot in a container in Nevada and the militiaman with a tablet in Sudan. Arendt watched Eichmann and worried about evil done at a desk. The machine in this week's headlines cuts, watches, carries and sells from a desk, and the rules it is breaking are older than the people flying it.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: For one night the whole world agreed about a football.
readings.claim: Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or appears in the headlines of Portugal, Colombia, Russia, Turkey, Senegal, Jordan, Greece, Spain and Nigeria within the same hours. No war, election or market event in this collection is reported by as many countries. A ceremony is the thing the world shares. The question is whether a shared ceremony is a kind of shared fate, or a substitute for one.

rungs.label: The one headline every country ran

fragments.label: Kane in nine countries
fragments.text: SAPO in Lisbon, La Patria in Manizales, Lenta in Moscow, Habertürk in Istanbul, Dakaractu in Dakar, Ammon in Amman and the Daily Post in Lagos all lead sport, and sometimes the whole page, with the same man and the same trophy. Nothing else in the collection crosses that many borders unchanged.

fragments.label: Each country finds its own loser
fragments.text: Russia's two outlets lead not with Kane but with Safonov missing out on the goalkeeper award. Nigeria lists five players shockingly omitted. Spain, Portugal and Colombia give Alexia Putellas her third. The world agreed on the ceremony and then each country read its own grievance or pride into the same list. That is what an imagined community does with a shared text.

rungs.label: The other things the world is sharing this week

fragments.label: Halloween is argued about on three continents
fragments.text: A Taipei fortune teller warns against dressing as one thing. A New Zealand broadcaster asks if Halloween is too scary for children. Houston explains how to elevate your wig. Texans pay two thousand dollars to have pumpkins arranged on the porch. An invented American tradition is now a global argument, held in the same week, in four languages.

fragments.label: The same obituary in Manila and Berlin
fragments.text: Walter Koenig of Star Trek dies at ninety and the Manila Times and Die Welt both report it. The voice of Bugs Bunny dies at forty-six and Córdoba asks what happened. Fortnite and One Piece join forces and Mexico tells you when. The world's shared dead and shared toys are American and Japanese, and nobody finds that remarkable.

rungs.label: What the crowd wants is to be one crowd

fragments.label: Four hundred thousand hosts and a navy band
fragments.text: Córdoba is preparing a papal Mass with 150 musicians, 2,000 communion ministers and 400,000 hosts. A navy band moves a crowd in Thessaloniki's main square. A Japanese editorial celebrates the prefecture's choirs. A French health centre runs a choir for mental health. Canetti said the crowd's deepest wish is to stop being many and become one. Every one of these headlines is that wish being granted for an hour.

fragments.label: A ceremony is cheaper than a fate
fragments.text: Debord's point was never that spectacle is trivial. It is that spectacle is what a society shares when it cannot share anything else. The same collection in which nine countries agree about Kane contains no headline that nine countries share about Sudan, water or the price of bread. We have a shared stadium and separate weather.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: The collector likes sport
fragments.text: This collection caps each country at eighteen headlines and samples what GDELT saw in ten minutes of a given hour. Sport is published on a predictable schedule and the ceremony fell inside the window. The 'one headline every country ran' may be an artefact of when the net was cast, not of what the world cares about. Run the same reading on a Tuesday morning and see if it holds.

fragments.label: A shared ceremony is not a lesser thing
fragments.text: The reading treats shared ritual as a consolation prize for shared fate. Weil would say the opposite: a people that can agree about a football, a choir and a Mass has roots, and roots are the condition for facing fate together, not the substitute. The oracle's disdain for the trophy might be the oracle's problem.

horizons.text: Live sport is the last thing a whole population watches at the same minute, and the decade's money has followed that fact. Streaming broke television into pieces between 2016 and 2026, so broadcasters paid more for the one thing that cannot be watched later. The Gulf states bought in: Qatar's World Cup in 2022, built by workers from Nepal, India and Bangladesh under a labour system the tournament was supposed to reform; Saudi Arabia's fund taking Newcastle in 2021, Ronaldo in 2022 and the World Cup of 2034. In April 2021 twelve clubs tried to leave for a closed Super League and were beaten in forty-eight hours by their own supporters, the one time in the decade a crowd won against capital. The Ballon d'Or became a stage for national grievance: Real Madrid boycotted the ceremony of 2024 when its player lost, and this week Russia reads the list for its goalkeeper and Nigeria for its omitted five. Halloween travelled the same networks, pumpkin-porch services in Texas and fortune-tellers in Taipei in the same week. What spreads now is the ceremony, not the meaning.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: Fifty years ago a football ceremony in Paris could not be watched in Lagos or Dakar on the night. The World Cup of 1970 was the first in colour by satellite, Live Aid in 1985 the first show built to be seen by a billion people at once, and the Premier League and Champions League of 1992 turned European club football into a product sold by the season. The Bosman ruling of 1995 is the migration story: by letting players move freely at the end of a contract, a European court turned national leagues into a global labour market, which is why a Senegalese paper and a Colombian one both have a stake in a trophy decided in Paris. FIFA under Havelange expanded the tournament to Africa and Asia and sold the rights to pay for it; the indictments of 2015 showed what the rights had paid for. Halloween's export began with Hollywood in the same decades, E.T. in 1982 doing for trick-or-treat what Coca-Cola had done for Santa Claus. Debord wrote in 1967 that the spectacle is capital accumulated to the point where it becomes an image. In 2026 nine countries own a share of the image and none of them owns the club.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: After 2001 the mass event became a security object and a marketing one in the same stroke. Stadiums got the airport's gates; broadcasters got a second screen. Twitter arrived in 2006, and Germany's 7-1 over Brazil in 2014 was for a while the most discussed thing that had ever happened on it: the shared text now came with a shared margin of comments in every language, which is what Russia's goalkeeper headline and Nigeria's omitted five are. The Premier League's audience in West Africa grew from viewing centres with satellite dishes into a national pastime, so a Lagos list of snubs is not foreign news but local. States noticed that the one thing everyone watches was for sale: Abu Dhabi bought Manchester City in 2008, Qatar bought Paris Saint-Germain in 2011, and the word sportswashing entered the dictionary. The shared canon shifted too. The deaths that cross borders this week, a Star Trek actor and the voice of Bugs Bunny, belong to the American television of the 1960s; the toys that cross them, Fortnite and One Piece, are an American game and a Japanese comic. Anderson's newspaper has become a console, and it is still read in the morning.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: The Ballon d'Or was invented in 1956 by a Paris magazine for the best European player, a year after the European Cup and a year before the Treaty of Rome. Football's Europe preceded the political one, and it was built for the same reason: to give people who had just fought each other something to meet about on a Wednesday night. Canetti finished Crowds and Power in 1960 with the fascist rally still in view; the postwar stadium was the answer to that fear, a crowd that forms and dissolves on a timetable and demands nothing afterwards. Television then made the crowd national and later global. Dayan and Katz called such broadcasts media events, the coronation and the moon landing, the moments when a society watches itself watching. The question Weil asked in 1949, what roots a people needs in order to bear a common fate, is the question the break rung raises against this reading. Seventy years of Wednesday nights have produced a shared ceremony across nine countries. Whether that is a root or a substitute for one is the thing this collection cannot settle, and the thing the whole postwar project of culture as peace has never settled either.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: Courts are re-sentencing 1979 and 1996, and a library is removing 2026.
readings.claim: Forty-seven years to the day after a KCIA chief shot South Korea's president, a court opens his posthumous retrial. Chile's Valparaíso court overturns a 1996 double-murder sentence. Milan rules on premeditation in a femicide. The same day, an Indian institute removes a living author's book from its library to avoid unrest. The past is being reopened everywhere, and the present is being shelved.

rungs.label: Old verdicts are being reopened

fragments.label: Why did he shoot the president?
fragments.text: Hankyoreh: he killed Korea's president 47 years ago, and a posthumous retrial may finally answer why. The collection was gathered on 26 October, the anniversary of the shooting. A country is asking a court to tell it whether the man who ended a dictatorship was a murderer or a liberator, and the man is not alive to hear the answer.

fragments.label: Valparaíso and Milan rewrite two sentences
fragments.text: A Chilean court dismisses the 'Drum Psychopath' double-murder case from 1996. Milan's ruling finds premeditation in Giulia Tramontano's killing, and the prosecutor-general calls it horrible. One court loosens the past, one tightens it. Both say the first telling was wrong.

rungs.label: The present is being taken off the shelf

fragments.label: A library removes a book to keep the peace
fragments.text: IISER Pune removes Umar Khalid's book from its library 'to avoid unrest'. Rahul Gandhi is acquitted in a defamation case the same day. One institution decides that a living writer's argument is too dangerous to lend, while a court decides that a politician's argument was legal. India is adjudicating speech in both directions at once.

fragments.label: A colonel's promise, a century later
fragments.text: Scoop: the colonel said they were safe as London, and nine men died by morning. In France, a Roman house and possible temple are found under a city. Kitakyushu concrete falls from a municipal wall onto a schoolboy. What was buried or guaranteed keeps surfacing, and it surfaces as a headline rather than a history.

rungs.label: Against revision: the people who simply stayed

fragments.label: Thirty-nine years, six months and two weeks
fragments.text: La Dépêche gives Alain Arnosti a send-off after thirty-nine years, six months and two weeks at one firm. A Virginia hospital volunteer marks fifty-five years. Rostock marks thirty years of support for the homeless. Edinburgh axes its Christmas ice rink after thirty. These are the headlines about time that no court can revise: the slow kind, where the verdict is just that someone kept turning up.

fragments.label: A ski brand revives a slogan, a daycare takes a 120-year-old building
fragments.text: Colmar revives its historic 'In case of snow' slogan for Austria's ski team. Vaasa turns a 120-year-old building into a daycare. Boym would call the first restorative nostalgia, rebuilding the old thing as it was, and the second reflective, letting the old thing hold something new. One is a marketing decision and one is a town's.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: Courts reopen cases every day
fragments.text: Appeals, retrials and acquittals are the ordinary business of justice, and a snapshot of 448 headlines will always contain some. The anniversary coincidence in Seoul is real, but the oracle has made a pattern out of a legal system functioning. The claim that 'the past is being reopened everywhere' would need a count across editions, and this is edition one.

fragments.label: Removing a book is censorship, not revision
fragments.text: Putting the Pune library beside the Seoul retrial makes them rhyme, and the rhyme flatters the reading. A retrial reopens the record. Removing a book closes it. They are opposite acts, and calling them both 're-sentencing' hides the one that matters more.

horizons.text: The decade reopened the record by every available means. Statues came down from Cape Town in 2015 to Bristol in 2020; from October 2017, #MeToo reopened cases that prosecutors had closed, and courts then re-closed some of them. Korea rewrote its own 1979 and 1980 twice over: a film about the December 1979 coup drew thirteen million viewers in 2023, a president declared martial law in December 2024 and was removed within four months, and the family of the man who shot Park Chung-hee won a retrial that opens, by these headlines, on the anniversary of the shooting. Italy answered a wave of femicides by moving to write the word into its criminal code; the Milan ruling on premeditation is part of that redefinition of an old crime. India's decade ran the other way. Umar Khalid has been held without trial since 2020, and an institute now removes his book to avoid unrest in the same week a court acquits a politician of defamation. Boym distinguished the nostalgia that rebuilds from the nostalgia that reflects. The decade's courts have done both, and its libraries have started to do neither.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: Fifty years ago a state that tried its own former rulers was almost unknown. Argentina did it first, in 1985, putting the juntas in a Buenos Aires courtroom two years after they left; Chile chose a commission in 1991 and did not reach its general until a London arrest in 1998 made the past prosecutable anywhere. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission of 1996 offered amnesty for testimony. Korea tried two former presidents in 1996 for the coup of 1979 and the Gwangju massacre, sentenced one to death, and pardoned both the following year; the retrial opening this week is the unfinished business of that first attempt. Ricoeur's book on memory came out in 2000 at the height of this age of transitional justice, when it seemed every country would eventually hold its own Nuremberg. The other headlines in this reading belong to a quieter fifty-year change. Thirty-nine years at one firm, fifty-five as a hospital volunteer, thirty years of a Christmas rink: these are the tenures of the postwar job and the postwar town, and their appearance as news measures how rare they have become since the flexible labour market arrived in the 1980s.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: The International Criminal Court opened in 2002, and for a decade it looked as if the reopening of the past would be institutionalised worldwide. It was, but by other means: the archive stopped closing. Everything written since 2001 is searchable, so a 1996 case, a 2020 arrest and a 2023 killing are all equally present, and a court's revision is compared at once with the first telling. Europe answered with the right to be forgotten in 2014, Spain with memory laws in 2007 and 2022 and the exhumation of Franco in 2019. The counter-movement is the ban. American school libraries removed thousands of titles between 2021 and 2024; India's 2019 amendments to its anti-terror law made it possible to hold a writer for years without a verdict, and the Pune institute is applying the same logic to a shelf. The two halves of this reading are the two halves of the post-2001 settlement with the past: the state can reopen any verdict, and the state can close any book. The library's decision and the court's were made on the same assumption, that memory is a security matter.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: Postwar Europe, in Judt's account, was built on an agreed forgetting. Nuremberg tried twenty-two men, denazification ran out of energy by 1949, and West Germany did not put its own citizens in the dock for Auschwitz until Frankfurt in 1963. Japan's trials ended in 1948, and Korea, divided in the same decade, dissolved the committee investigating colonial collaborators in 1949 before it had finished. Jaspers argued in 1946 that guilt could be criminal, political, moral or metaphysical, and that a court could handle only the first. Every retrial since is an attempt to make a court handle the others. The man Seoul is retrying ended a dictatorship and was hanged for it, and the question the court is asked, whether he was a murderer or a liberator, is a Jaspers question dressed as a verdict. The Chilean, Italian and Indian headlines are the same postwar machinery in three settings: a state that promised never again, and then had to decide, case by case, what the promise covered. Seventy years on the deciding has not slowed. It has become the daily work of courts, and this collection caught one day of it.
horizons.label: Since 1945

readings.line: Students have toppled a government, and a president is doing a teenage dance.
readings.claim: In Serbia a leaderless movement of the young has ended fourteen years of Vučić. In France the government promises to reform university admissions after mass student protests. In Madrid a camp refuses to leave Sol. In Antioquia three towns decree that minors be kept indoors. And in Buenos Aires the 56-year-old president joins the 'Six Seven' teenage challenge. The generation in the square is being answered by reform, curfew and imitation, and the imitation is the most revealing of the three.

rungs.label: The square is full

fragments.label: Belgrade: young, leaderless, without experience, and they won
fragments.text: El País describes the movement that defeated Vučić's regime as young, leaderless and without political experience. Il Messaggero asks who they are and calls it a turning point after fourteen years. A quarter-century after the Otpor students, Serbia's students have done it again, and the foreign press cannot decide whether to be impressed or alarmed by the absence of a leader.

fragments.label: Paris reforms, Madrid camps, Lisbon argues about the police
fragments.text: France pledges to reform university admissions after mass student protests, reported from Córdoba. Madrid's Sol protesters shield their camp and say there is no retreat. In Lisbon the mayor stands with housing protesters but will not comment on the police, the communists reject 'subterfuges to limit' the right to protest, and Ventura demands that Seguro break his silence. Three capitals, three responses to the same crowd.

rungs.label: Elsewhere the answer is a curfew and a metric

fragments.label: Antioquia keeps the young indoors
fragments.text: El Colombiano: three towns decree that minors be kept indoors as a solution to violence. Brazilian students protest outside São Paulo's City Hall. Peru's teachers confirm a national strike. Where Belgrade's young filled the square, Antioquia's are told the square is the danger.

fragments.label: Ninety-seven applicants per place
fragments.text: China's civil service exam reaches 97 applicants per place. Sydney's selective schools are sending students to the psychologist under parental pressure. A Vietnamese editorial says do not let talent be constrained by metrics. A Colombian blog asks whose childhood is being published. The young who are not in the square are in a queue, and the queue is measured.

rungs.label: The imitation is the tell

fragments.label: A president does the dance
fragments.text: Minuto Uno explains what 'Six Seven' means: the teenage challenge Javier Milei joined at 56. Power is not only reforming, policing or measuring the young. It is dressing as them. Krastev and Holmes wrote about nations imitating other nations. This is a government imitating its own children, which is the version that happens when the children have the numbers.

fragments.label: Four hundred thousand hosts and a generation that may not come
fragments.text: Cadena 3 reports what Argentines expect from the pope's historic visit, and names the contrast with young people. Seven in ten Koreans aged 60 to 74 say they are not elderly and want more chances to take part. The old are declining to be old and the young are declining to be counted. The square and the Mass are competing for the same bodies.

rungs.label: Break this reading

fragments.label: 'The young' is not a political actor
fragments.text: Serbian students, Colombian minors, Chinese exam candidates and a Buenos Aires meme have nothing in common except age, and age is not a programme. The reading assembles a generation out of headlines because generation is an easy story. Ask what each group wants and the constellation falls apart into housing, exams, violence and attention.

fragments.label: The last springtime lasted a year
fragments.text: Every wave of the young in the square is reported as a turning point, and 1848 is the reminder that most turning points turn back. Belgrade's 2000 victory produced the Vučić the students have just removed. The oracle's excitement is the same excitement the newspapers had then. The honest reading of this collection is that we are in the first week, and the first week always looks like this.

horizons.text: The decade's square was Hong Kong's in 2019, Santiago's the same October when students jumped the metro turnstiles and started a constitutional process the country later voted down twice, and Tehran's in 2022. Then the young began to win. Sri Lankan crowds removed a president in 2022; Bangladeshi students removed a prime minister in August 2024 after protests over job quotas; Kenya's Gen Z forced the withdrawal of a finance bill in June 2024; Nepal's forced out a government in September 2025 under a pirate flag from a Japanese comic. Serbia's students began with a station canopy in Novi Sad and ended, by these headlines, with Vučić. The other decade belongs to the queue. China stopped publishing its youth unemployment rate in 2023 when it passed a fifth; the civil service exam now has ninety-seven applicants a place; Korea became a super-aged society in December 2024, with a fifth of its people over sixty-five. Where the young are many they fill the square. Where they are few they fill the exam hall, and a president dances for them because they are a swing vote rather than a crowd.
horizons.label: The past decade

horizons.text: Students have been ending governments for exactly fifty years. Soweto in June 1976 began the end of apartheid; students carried the Iranian revolution in 1978, died at Gwangju in 1980, won Korea's democracy in June 1987, filled Tiananmen in 1989 and lost, marched in Prague that November and won, forced out Suharto in May 1998 and Milošević in October 2000. The pattern tracks demography. In 1976 the median age in South Africa, Iran and Korea was under twenty-two; the young were the majority and the square was theirs. Korea's median age is now above forty-five and Italy's and Spain's are higher, and the squares in Madrid and Lisbon this week are about housing, the one issue on which the postwar compact between generations has visibly broken: the people who bought in the 1970s own, the people born after 1990 rent. Serbia's students are the exception that proves it, a young movement in an ageing country, which is why the foreign press cannot read them. Hirschman's exit is the other half-century story: the young of the countries in the queue have been leaving, and Lisbon's housing crisis is partly made of the people who arrived.
horizons.label: The past fifty years

horizons.text: The post-2001 square has a short, repeating life. More than ten million people marched against the Iraq war on one weekend in February 2003, the largest protest there had ever been, and changed nothing. In 2011 a Tunisian vegetable seller set himself alight and within months Tahrir Square, Puerta del Sol and Zuccotti Park were occupied by people in their twenties with no leaders and a hashtag. Madrid's camp this week is in the same square as the one of May 2011, and its slogan, no retreat, is an answer to what happened last time: the indignados became a party, the party entered government, and the rents went up. Egypt's spring became a general by 2013, Syria's a war, Tunisia's a president who dissolved parliament in 2021. Gezi in 2013 and Maidan in 2014 produced, respectively, a more entrenched leader and an invasion. The lesson the young of 2026 have drawn is visible in Belgrade: no leader to arrest, no party to co-opt, and a demand narrow enough to be met. Krastev and Holmes wrote about the humiliation of imitating. A government that dances the children's dance has moved from imitation to flattery, which is what power does once it has counted the room.
horizons.label: Since September 2001

horizons.text: The young as a political actor is a postwar invention. The baby boom, full employment and the expansion of universities produced, by the 1960s, the first generation that was numerous, educated, free in the mornings and in the same place. 1968 followed: Paris in May, Prague in August, Mexico City in October, where the army fired on students ten days before the Olympics, and campuses from Berkeley to Tokyo. The responses available to states were set then and have not changed: reform the university, as France did within the year and promises to do again this week; close the square, as Mexico did and as three towns in Antioquia are doing with a curfew; or borrow the costume, as every politician since Nixon on a comedy show in 1968 has tried. Hobsbawm thought the cultural revolution of the 1960s was the most lasting thing the century produced, more than any regime. The square in Belgrade, the camp in Sol and the dance in Buenos Aires are its three legacies in one week. 1848 is in the library for the same reason: the springtime of peoples lasted a year, and its ideas lasted a century.
horizons.label: Since 1945
